newsitem.title: CHINA: Yuan ends up as central bank eases intervention.
newsitem.headline: Yuan ends up as central bank eases intervention.

text.p: The Chinese yuan closed slightly firmer against the U.S. dollar on Tuesday, and dealers said the local unit was aided by central bank cautiousness following weeks of Southeast Asian currency turmoil.

Dealers said the central bank -- which had been selling yuan for dollars in a bid to slow the advance of the local currency until recently -- had turned more cautious due to the weakness of Southeast Asian currencies on international markets.
The yuan ended at its intraday high of 8.2900 to the U.S. dollar in Shanghai on Tuesday from Monday's 8.2902.

"After the sharp depreciation of currencies in Southeast Asia, the People's Bank of China has reduced its intervention to depress the yuan to ensure there is no opportunity for speculators to force the currency down," one dealer said.
"The central bank now wants to keep the yuan moving in a narrow range to avoid risks brought by speculative buying," another dealer said.

Speculators have only a limited chance to push the local currency around as the unit is not fully convertible. China also has a large supply of dollars due to its trade surplus and an influx of investment capital.

The weighted average price on Monday was 8.2903. The yuan opened unchanged at 8.2902 and moved in a range of 8.2902/8.2905 for most of the session, touching an intraday low of 8.2908 before the close. Trading was more active than on Monday, dealers said.
"Buying of the yuan pushed the local currency up to test the key resistance level of 8.2900 again," one dealer said.
"The rise was capped by selling at the 8.2900 level most probably from the central bank today," he said.
Dealers said the yuan should breach the 8.2900 level on Wednesday. The yuan ended higher at 7.0526 from 7.0799 against 100 Japanese yen and at 1.0700 from 1.0702 to the Hong Kong dollar.
